Now imagine that these are the players' computer programs.
With this idea, multi-agent reinforcement learning begins.
In reinforcement learning, an agent is the system that takes action in the environment.
The environment is the world or the situation where the agent is working.
The agent gets information, then he chooses action.
After action, he gets reward or penalty.
Gradually, the agent learns which action is useful in which situation.
A robot is in the maze. If he goes near the exit, he gets reward and if he hits the wall, then penalty.
Now, place a lot of agents instead of an agent.
From here, multi-agent reinforcement learning or killing comes.
Every agent understands the world from their observations and takes action according to their policy.
Policy is a rule or strategy that tells what I should do in this situation.
In the multi-agent system, other agents are also taking actions.
That is why the environment is changing every time.
Agent is not only giving the response of walls, roads or rewards.
He is also giving the response of other intelligent agents' decisions.
The response of agents is also giving.
Shared environment means that agents share only space, resources or rules.
In the warehouse, robots use only one isle.
Cars walk on the same roads in traffic.
If two robots want to go to the same charging station,
then competition is born.
If both choose different routes and complete deliveries,
then cooperation is seen.
In cooperation, agents have a common goal.
The goal of rescue drones can be covered by more areas.
Every drone chooses its own route,
but the final objective is of the team.
In competition, the goal of agents is often the opposite.
In chess, one player wins and the other loses.
In strategy games, two teams compete for the same resources and territory.
The competition agent teaches to predict the behavior of the opponent.
If you only learn your best moves and ignore the opponent, then the policy can fail quickly.
In multi-agent setting, the environment looks non-stationary.
This means that the strategy against which the agent was learning is also changing.
If one player improves defense, the other will change attack.
Every agent makes others better.
In some problems, cooperation and competition are both the same.
Team mates cooperate in the game and compete against opposing team.
Now let's come to the credit assignment.
The question of credit assignment is, did the team get a reward?
But in this reward, what was the contribution of which agent?
Imagine that four robots move to a heavy box.
The team got a reward because it reached the box destination.
But one robot gave direction, the other one pushed the box, the third one cleared the way
and the fourth one was almost doing nothing.
If everyone gets the same reward, then inactive robot can also learn successful behavior.
If only the pushing robot gets the reward, then the contribution of the robot giving direction
can be missed.
That is why shared reward and individual reward can be both useful.
Shared reward shows team success.
Individual reward guides the local action of the agent.
The balance of both the rewards is important.
Otherwise, an agent can be selfish or he doesn't understand his role.
Another issue is the delayed reward. Sometimes action is taken now, but the result is very late.
A drone chose a route first, then the team got a target after 10 minutes.
Now the system has to understand which decision helped in success.
This is called a temporal credit assignment.
Human teams can give manager feedback.
They can say that your planning was useful, your timing was good and your communication was weak.
AI agents don't get such detailed feedback naturally.
They have to estimate the contribution from the reward signal.
If the reward is too late, the learning can be slow.
That is why useful systems, intermediate signals and sub-goals are also used.
Partial observability is also common in goods.
Every agent can only see a part of the environment.
A rescue robot can see its corridor, but not the other robot's corridor.
If the robot wants to understand other people's actions,
it will have to assume hidden information.
You will have to think about it. Memory and communication can reduce this problem.
One robot can tell you that the left corridor has already been searched.
The other robot can use their time in a new area.
Even without communication, cooperation is possible.
Agents can observe other people's actions and guess their intentions.
But learning from communication can be fast.
It is not necessary to tell each agent everything.
It is only necessary to share that information which improves the team's results.
multi-agent reinforcement learning can be used in the real world.
First of all, traffic management.
If traffic lights are understood by different agents,
then every signal can observe its nearby traffic.
But the best result will be when signals coordinate.
If one signal only reduces the wait time of its road,
then traffic can be jammed on the other road.
The shared goal should be the smooth flow of the network.
Second example is the warehouse robots.
Every robot picks and delivers packages.
If robots learn routes, they can avoid busy aisles.
With cooperation, robots divide tasks.
With competition, there can be conflict for charging stations or short routes.
To avoid collision, to meet deadlines and to save energy,
one has to learn together.
The third example is of drones.
Many drones are searching for a large area.
If every drone takes a random route,
it can be scanned again and again.
If the agents observe each other's routes
observe and share information, then coverage can be better. If a drone detects an object,
then it can be useful to send the remaining drones to that location.
In MARL, the idea of centralized training and decentralized execution is also used.
During training, the system can see information of all the agents.
It is easy to learn team coordination from this. But during actual operation,
each agent only takes action from their local observations.
action.

There are some important limitations of the route.
The first limitation is sample efficiency.
Agents may need a lot of trials to learn a useful strategy.
With real robots, every trial can be expensive and risky.
Agents can be fast trained in simulation, but there is a difference between simulation
and reality.
This difference is called SIM2 real gap.
The second limitation is scalability.
If the number of agents increases, then the possible interactions become too much.
In the case of 100 agents, each agent's second
agents' behavior model can be difficult. Third limitation is reward design. If a delivery
robot is given a speed reward, then it can ignore safety. It is necessary to carefully align
the reward with desired behavior.
Fourth limitation is explainability. Sometimes teams are successful, but we are not clear
on which hidden pattern the agent has learned. In safety critical systems,
there is not enough result. Engineers also have to understand why the decision was taken.
So, communication rules, role-based policies and monitoring are important.
The mall system should not only maximize reward, it should follow safety constraints.
If many robots are in a narrow corridor, then before fast delivery,
it is important to avoid collision.
A good multi-agent system balances its actions with team goals, local information
and safety rules.

What is the core idea of single-agent learning?
In a shared environment, many agents learn from observations,
choose actions through policies,
take feedback from rewards,

The most difficult part is that

In single-agent learning, the system learns from its environment,
but in multi-agent learning, the system also learns from other learners.
The real world is not a collection of independent machines.
Cars share roads, robots share warehouses, drones share information.
Humans and AI systems take decisions in one environment.
Finally, think about it. When many intelligent agents work together,
then the most important thing is intelligence or better coordination.
Perhaps the powerful systems of the future will be the ones that are not only

Let's take a detailed example of a team game.
Three agents are in a digital field.
The first agent observes the opponent,
the second finds a safe route,
and the third completes the objective.
If the three do their work independently,
then duplication and confusion can be done.
But if their policies are according to the role,
then the team can be efficient.
The first agent shares information,
the second plans a route,
and the third executes action.

Not just one direction. Cooperation means that every agent should understand their roles and support the actions of other agents.
In this example, rewards should not only be for the final objective.
Sharing information, avoiding collisions, and useful feedback for the correct timing.
There is a problem of learning stability in the moral.
One agent improves his policy, but other agents are also updating their policies.
This is why behavior that was useful yesterday can fail today.
Think that one driver chooses routes in traffic.
If all drivers choose the same route, then that route will slow down.
Then some drivers choose another route and traffic pattern will change again.
Intelligent agents' decisions continuously change the environment.
This is why agents should not learn fixed rules.
They should learn to observe other's behavior,
handle uncertainty and adapt to changing conditions.

Communication can be the central part of moral, but unlimited communication is not practical.
If every agent shares every information, then the system can be noisy and slow.
So, the agents have to learn when to send a message, which agent to send, and what to tell in the message.
The warehouse robot can share its exact position, but not every sensor reading.
The rescue drone can share target location and confidence.
It can understand selective communication.
The goal of communication is not to send too many messages, but to give useful information at the right time.
If the message comes late, then the decision can be missed.
If the message is wrong, the entire team's policy can be disturbed.
That is why trust, message verification and communication cost can also be a part of learning.
Every reinforcement learning system has to balance between exploration and exploitation.
Exploration means trying a new action. Exploitation means using that action
which has already been useful. Exploration becomes more difficult in multi-agent settings.
If a robot tries a new route, its effect can affect other robots as well.
If a player tests a new strategy in the game, the team's results can be temporarily weak.
That's why safe exploration is important in real world marbles.
Agents should not try every risky action freely.
Through simulations, safety limits and human supervision,
the system can be given a control learning environment.
